title: Whatever happened to acid rain?
summary: Josh and Chuck explain acid rain: what it is (sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide emissions reacting with water vapor to form sulfuric and nitric acid, wet and dry deposition), the pH scale and why normal rain is slightly acidic, ecosystem damage to plankton, lakes, soil, trees and coastal waters, health and material effects like corrosion of statues and car paint, the history from Robert Angus Smith's 1872 coinage through the 1980 Acid Deposition Act and 1990 Clean Air Act amendments, the cap-and-trade system that cut sulfur dioxide emissions, and the remaining recovery. The episode also includes listener mail about Comic-Con plans, an MIT listener's correction about MIT's Engineers nickname and beaver mascot, an engineer joke, and a request for listeners' meaning of "chocolate rain."

entities.name: Clean Air Status and Trends Network

segments.title: Opening banter and 1980s environmental fears
segments.summary: Hosts banter about the Dejounte-era song reference, recall 1980s fears about the ozone hole and acid rain, and note that acid rain has been largely addressed while the ozone hole has not.

segments.title: What acid rain is and how it forms
segments.summary: Acid rain is rain with acid from sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides (from cars, factories, power plants, and natural sources like lightning and volcanoes) that react with water vapor to form sulfuric and nitric acid. It can be wet or dry deposition, called acid deposition.

segments.title: The pH scale and normal rain
segments.summary: The hosts explain the pH scale, with pure water near neutral, and note that normal rain is slightly acidic around 5.6 because of carbonic acid from carbon dioxide. Acid rain falls around 4.3 to 5, comparable to orange juice or black coffee, though that comparison is misleading.

segments.title: Effects on plankton, fish and food chains
segments.summary: Acid rain harms sensitive organisms like plankton, which die off and starve larger animals such as fish and frogs. The hosts also cover the monitoring programs in the US (National Atmospheric Deposition Program and Clean Air Status and Trends Network) and the concept of critical load.
topics: Clean Air Status and Trends Network

segments.title: Soil buffering, lakes and coastal nitrogen
segments.summary: Soil normally buffers acid with minerals like calcium, but when its buffering capacity is overloaded, acid flows into water bodies. Nitrogen from acid rain fuels algae blooms in coastal waters, which leads to oxygen depletion and harm to fish and shellfish.

segments.title: Forests, aluminum, health and material damage
segments.summary: Acid rain draws aluminum out of soil, which tree roots can absorb as a toxin, and strips minerals needed by trees. At higher elevations acid fog strips leaves, causing bald peaks in the Appalachians. Dry deposition combined with ozone and VOCs creates smog harmful to respiratory health, and acid corrodes stone monuments and car paint.

segments.title: History: Robert Angus Smith and the 1970s-1990 policy response
segments.summary: Robert Angus Smith coined the term acid rain in 1872 after seeing damaged monuments. Scientists in the 1970s found acid rain was transboundary. The Acid Deposition Act set a ten-year study, and in 1990 Congress added sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides to the Clean Air Act's reduction list.

segments.title: Cap and trade and recovery results
segments.summary: A cap-and-trade system for sulfur dioxide from power plants, with tradeable allowances, cut emissions substantially. Nitrogen oxide cap and trade started around 2003 with emissions falling from 27 million tons in 1980 to 16.3 million in 2008. Acidic lakes in Wisconsin, Michigan, the Adirondacks and Northern Appalachians have declined, though recovery is incomplete.

segments.title: Comic-Con announcement and MIT listener mail
segments.summary: The hosts announce they will attend Comic-Con in San Diego in July. A listener from MIT corrects the hosts on the school's nickname (Engineers, not eggheads), its beaver mascot, and course numbering, and the hosts read an engineer joke.

segments.title: Chocolate rain request and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts ask listeners what 'chocolate rain' means, give contact details for the show, and sign off with a promotional ad line.
